title: The terminal: how to navigate, move files, read files
story:
The Teletype Model 33, an electromechanical teleprinter introduced in 1963, was widely used as a computer terminal. Interaction was a line of typed text sent to the machine and a line of printed text sent back, on paper. There was no screen to redraw, no cursor to move, and nothing that could be revised once printed — so the conversation could only be a sequence of lines.

Worth correcting a commonly repeated claim about what replaced it. The mouse was invented by Douglas Engelbart at the Stanford Research Institute and demonstrated publicly in December 1968 — not at Xerox. What Xerox did was the Alto, built at its Palo Alto research centre in 1973, which established the graphical user interface as it is now understood by combining windows, icons and a mouse on one machine. The distinction matters because the usual telling gives one organisation credit for both the device and the interface, and the interesting contribution is the second: assembling existing parts into something coherent.

The shells preserved the older shape rather than the older hardware. The Bourne shell was written by Stephen Bourne at Bell Labs and released in the seventh edition of Unix in 1979; Bash was written by Brian Fox and first released in 1989.

Here is the part that makes this history relevant rather than decorative. A constraint imposed by a printer turned out to be a superior composition model, and it outlived its cause by decades.

Because every program reads a stream of text and writes a stream of text, any program's output can become any other program's input. That is one rule, and it means programs written years apart by people who never communicated can be combined by someone who understands neither. List files, filter the list, count what remains — three tools, connected, producing something none of them was built to do. Nothing in graphical computing has an equivalent, because there is no general way to connect the output of one window to the input of another.

The commands themselves are worth stating as a set rather than individually, since the set is small. Move between directories, list what is in one, copy, move and remove, read a file whole or a page at a time, search within files, and find files by name. That is most of it. The rest is combination.

The cost of composition through untyped text should be named, because the advantage gets taught without it. Every program in a chain must parse the previous one's output, and that output is a convention rather than a contract — a change in the format of one tool breaks every chain that consumed it, with no error until something downstream misreads a column. Text is universal precisely because it carries no structure, and carrying no structure is also why nothing can check that two tools agree.

The practical argument for learning this is narrower than reverence for tradition. When something is running on a machine you reached over the network, the graphical layer is often not there, and it is never there in the case where it matters — the one where the system is broken and you are trying to find out why. The interface that assumes the least about the machine is the one that still works when the machine is least well.

problem.move: Connect one program's output to the next one's input rather than looking for a tool that does the whole job. Where the chain depends on the shape of intermediate output, treat that shape as an assumption to verify, since it is a convention rather than a contract.
problem.invariant: If every program reads text and writes text, any program's output can be any other's input — which lets tools written independently compose without their authors having agreed on anything.
problem.breaks: Universality comes from carrying no structure, and carrying no structure is why nothing can check that two tools agree. A change in one tool's output format breaks every chain consuming it, with no error raised — just a downstream misreading.

problem.practice: Take a question about your own filesystem that no single command answers, and build it from three connected ones. Then change one tool in the chain for a similar one and watch what breaks — that is the cost of a convention rather than a contract.

beats.broke: Interaction was a line of text in and a line of text out because the hardware was a printer, and that shape was inherited by everything built on top of it.
beats.fix: Treat the constraint as a design: small programs reading and writing text compose by connecting one's output to another's input, so tools written independently combine without their authors having agreed on anything.
beats.cost: Composition through untyped text means every program parses the previous one's output, so the interface between two tools is a convention rather than a contract and a format change breaks chains silently.

interview.q: Why did a text stream interface outlive the hardware that forced it?
